newsitem.title: UK: Woolwich solid debut gives few clues on cash.
newsitem.headline: Woolwich solid debut gives few clues on cash.

text.p: British building society-turned-bank Woolwich Plc on Wednesday produced few surprises in its debut results but it kept the market thinking about what it will do with its surplus capital.

"We are actively working on how we can deploy excess capital to produce proper returns to shareholders... and we are looking at how we can return some to shareholders," Woolwich's finance director Robert Jeens told Reuters. Woolwich reported first half pre-tax profits of 187.8 million pounds ($305.1 million), compared with 183.1 million pounds for the same period in 1996.
Jeens said Woolwich had "considerably more money than we think it would be easy to spend" but had no intention of splashing its cash about. The bank has between 600 and 700 million pounds to spend.

"We are not going out with a cheque book, we are looking very carefully at things. As in the past we expect to spend typically quite small amounts of money but make absolutely sure that is going to make us good returns," Jeens said.
Woolwich also was watching how the British tax regime may change in the period before the group's annual meeting next year, when it plans to put proposals on returning cash to shareholders.
"We've got to make sure that whatever we propose to shareholders makes good sense to them, and tax is a big issue there," he added.
Woolwich shares reacted positively to the results, rising 4.5 pence to 296.5 pence by 0945 GMT, still a long way short of the 370 pence peak reached on the first day's trading.
The results were consistent with the bank's listing particulars at the end of May.

Woolwich's headline figure, excluding an exceptional cost of conversion of 26.7 million pounds, was up 13 percent at 215 million pounds. Operating costs dropped to 173.2 million pounds, from 178.8 million for the same period a year earlier.
Further conversion costs would appear in the group's full year results, with around 15 million pounds likely to cover advisors fees, distributing shares to institutions and other costs.

Woolwich, which shed a 150-year mutual tradition as a building society when it floated on the stock exchange on July 7, said it would pay an interim dividend of 3.0 pence per share, slightly above forecasts of 2.8-2.9 pence.
Analysts had forecast the pre-tax profits in a range of 180 to 185 million pounds.
"We are very much getting on with the job, we know what we have got to do and we are now hard at work actually doing that," Jeens said, adding the flotation process had been quite a distraction.

Woolwich said it recognised the increasingly competitive nature of the British personal financial services market and its continuing review of costs and operating processes was expected to contribute to further improvement in its cost to income ratio.
Group lending for the period fell to 636 million pounds, from 653 million pounds in the second half of 1996 and 995 million pounds in the first half of 1996.

Woolwich said figures for both the second half of 1996 and the first half of 1997 had been hit by the strength of sterling against continental currencies. This, said Jeens, had had an impact on Woolwich's French and Italian businesses.

Gross mortgage lending of 1,701 million pounds "represented a successful balance between meeting customers needs and maintaining appropriate financial returns" against the background of highly competitive market conditions, the bank said.
"In terms of UK net lending our share in the half year is very similar to the second half of last year," Jeens said. Woolwich's share was 4.6, down from five percent in the second half of 1996.

Jeens said Woolwich's natural market share was about 5.5 percent. He said the bank was striking a balance between those offering very competitive deals aimed at buying market share and others who were not doing any new business at all.

"We are not concerned with market share per se. What we are concerned with doing is looking after our customers so we maintain good profitable relationships with (them), we're striking that balance in the new business we're writing," he said.
Woolwich has no immediate plans to make any acquisitions, but will look for the right deal to deliver the right returns, Jeens said.
It is looking at growing its existing businesses more rapidly but organically, ventures with third parties and acquisitions.
But despite recent take-over speculation in Woolwich had not received any approaches from other institutions and was concentrating on its own plans.
"We're working on a number of areas. We are basically keen to broaden our portfolio," he added.
Provisions for bad or doubtful debts fell to 7.2 million pounds for the period, from 22.9 million pounds in the same period of 1996. ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
